topic: Joshua Greene (2001): Switch vs Footbridge — How Personal Moral Force Splits Emotional Alarm From Cold Utilitarian Math
visual_mode_reason: Greene's 2001 Princeton fMRI trolley experiment pairs two physical moral scenarios (pulling an impersonal railway switch vs pushing a bystander off a footbridge to save five lives) with dual-process competition between ventromedial prefrontal / amygdala alarm and dorsolateral prefrontal calculation.

primary_case.title: Joshua D. Greene, R. Brian Sommerville, Leigh E. Nystrom, John M. Darley & Jonathan D. Cohen's 2001 Science fMRI Trolley vs Footbridge study
primary_case.place: Center for the Study of Brain, Mind and Behavior, Princeton University

people.name: Joshua D. Greene
people.role: Princeton philosophy-turned-neuroscience researcher (later Harvard) who scanned subjects solving classic Switch vs Footbridge moral dilemmas

people.name: Jonathan D. Cohen & John M. Darley
people.role: Senior Princeton cognitive neuroscientist and social psychologist co-authors on the 2001 Science paper

people.name: Philippa Foot & Judith Jarvis Thomson
people.role: Moral philosophers who formulated the original 1967/1985 runaway trolley and footbridge thought experiments

core_facts.fact: Philosophers Philippa Foot (1967) and Judith Jarvis Thomson (1985) posed a baffling paradox: the arithmetic is identical — sacrifice 1 life to save 5 — yet roughly 80-90% of people endorse pulling a track switch ('Switch dilemma'), whereas ~80-90% refuse to push one person off a bridge onto the tracks ('Footbridge dilemma').

In 2001 at Princeton, Joshua Greene and colleagues scanned two cohorts of 9 volunteers each (18 total) in fMRI across 60 dilemmas split into Moral-Personal (Footbridge-style), Moral-Impersonal (Switch-style), and Non-Moral puzzles.

Moral-Personal dilemmas selectively lit up emotion- and social-cognition hubs — medial frontal gyrus / ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), posterior cingulate, and angular gyrus — far more strongly than Moral-Impersonal Switch dilemmas with the exact same 5-for-1 body count.
Conversely, Moral-Impersonal Switch dilemmas activated dorsolateral prefrontal and parietal working-memory circuits to virtually the same level as cold Non-Moral train-schedule math problems.

Reaction times exposed the hidden tug-of-war inside the skull: saying 'Appropriate' (riding WITH the gut alarm, e.g., pulling the impersonal switch) was fast, whereas overriding the emotional alarm to say 'Appropriate' on a Moral-Personal dilemma took ~2 seconds longer (~6.8 s vs ~4.9 s for 'Inappropriate').

In 2004 (Neuron), Greene showed anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) detects conflict between the gut alarm and the 5-vs-1 math, recruiting dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) on trials where subjects ultimately choose the utilitarian override.

Putting volunteers under heavy cognitive load (memorizing scrolling digits while deciding, Greene 2008) selectively slowed utilitarian 'yes' overrides without slowing deontological 'no' refusals — confirming utilitarian math requires effortful executive control.

Later replications and critiques (Greene 2009; Kahane et al.) clarified that 'personal muscular force used as an intentional means' — not mere spatial proximity — triggers the immediate vmPFC/amygdala veto, and patients with vmPFC lesions endorse pushing on the footbridge at dramatically elevated rates.

Thirty-four (34) years after Philippa Foot's 1967 tram problem, Greene et al. (2001) scanned participants inside fMRI and documented a ~85% verdict swing between impersonal switch and personal footbridge dilemmas despite identical 5-versus-1 arithmetic.

wow_facts.fact: Same math — 5 lives saved, 1 life lost — yet flipping an impersonal lever activates cold working-memory math circuits while using your own hands on a footbridge triggers an instant ventromedial emotional alarm.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Your brain runs two rival moral cameras: an automatic emotional alarm and a slow executive calculator.

wow_facts.fact: The handful of volunteers who STILL said 'Yes, push to save five' on personal dilemmas took nearly TWO FULL SECONDS longer to press the button — the exact time cost of dorsolateral cortex wrestling down their own gut veto.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Reaction time caught a philosophical civil war in milliseconds.

wow_facts.fact: Give people a 7-digit number to hold in memory while deciding (Greene 2008), and ONLY their utilitarian calculation slows down — emotional 'Never push!' answers fire just as fast.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Deontological alarm is automatic; utilitarian override burns working memory.

wow_facts.fact: Patients with focal damage to ventromedial prefrontal cortex calmly endorse pushing on the footbridge because the visceral alarm wire is silent while their 5-is-greater-than-1 calculator stays intact.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Lesion neurology confirmed fMRI dual-process predictions.

misconceptions.myth: Moral judgments come purely from conscious logical principles that we deduce first and feel second.
misconceptions.truth: Automatic socio-emotional alarm circuits fire first on personal force, and conscious principles often rationalize that gut verdict after the fact.

misconceptions.myth: Utilitarian '5 > 1' answers inside the scanner prove someone is wise and compassionate.
misconceptions.truth: High utilitarian scores on extreme sacrificial dilemmas can stem EITHER from effortful cognitive concern OR from blunted vmPFC/antisocial empathy — two opposite neural routes to the same button.

misconceptions.myth: Any physical touch makes a dilemma feel forbidden.
misconceptions.truth: Follow-up experiments (Greene 2009) proved it is the combination of 'personal muscular force' AND 'using harm as an intentional means' — not side-effect switch pulls — that trips the alarm.

everyday_hooks: Feeling totally fine donating to a statistical triage policy on paper, yet freezing when a single named patient looks you in the eye.
Understanding why hospital triage boards, self-driving car engineers, and emergency commanders separate frontline personal care from resource allocation formulas.
Noticing your own mind invent elaborate philosophical reasons two seconds AFTER an instant gut 'No way!'
